claim: Many developmental processes break left–right (LR) symmetry with a consistent handedness.
source: Many developmental processes break left–right (LR) symmetry with a consistent handedness.
evidence: This is a general statement about developmental biology supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: LR asymmetry emerges early in development.
source: LR asymmetry emerges early in development, and in many species the primary determinant of this asymmetry has been linked to the cytoskeleton.
evidence: Supported by citations in the manuscript to established literature.

claim: In many species the primary determinant of LR asymmetry has been linked to the cytoskeleton.
source: LR asymmetry emerges early in development, and in many species the primary determinant of this asymmetry has been linked to the cytoskeleton.
evidence: Supported by citations in the manuscript to established literature.

claim: The actomyosin cortex generates active chiral torques to facilitate chiral symmetry breaking.
source: In this study, we combine thin-film active chiral fluid theory with experimental analysis of the C. elegans embryo to show that the actomyosin cortex generates active chiral torques to facilitate chiral symmetry breaking.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data and theoretical modeling presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Active torques drive chiral counter-rotating cortical flow in the zygote.
source: Active torques drive chiral counter-rotating cortical flow in the zygote, depend on myosin activity, and can be altered through mild changes in Rho signaling.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and measurements presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: Active torques depend on myosin activity.
source: Active torques drive chiral counter-rotating cortical flow in the zygote, depend on myosin activity, and can be altered through mild changes in Rho signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through mlc-4 RNAi experiments showing reduction in chiral flow with reduced myosin activity.

claim: Active torques can be altered through mild changes in Rho signaling.
source: Active torques drive chiral counter-rotating cortical flow in the zygote, depend on myosin activity, and can be altered through mild changes in Rho signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through ect-2 and rga-3 RNAi experiments showing changes in chirality index.

claim: Active torques execute the chiral skew event at the 4-cell stage to establish the C. elegans LR body axis.
source: Notably, they also execute the chiral skew event at the 4-cell stage to establish the C. elegans LR body axis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between chiral flow and skew angle at the 4-cell stage.

claim: Most organisms are bilaterally asymmetric with morphologically distinct left and right hand sides.
source: Most organisms are bilaterally asymmetric with morphologically distinct left and right hand sides.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: Bilateral asymmetry of organisms, organs, and tissues emerges early in development and is dependent on chiral symmetry breaking of cells and subcellular structures.
source: Bilateral asymmetry of organisms, organs, and tissues emerges early in development and is dependent on chiral symmetry breaking of cells and subcellular structures (Hayashi and Murakami, 2001; Shibazaki et al., 2004; Danilchik et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2007; Hejnol, 2010; Tamada et al., 2010; Vandenberg and Levin, 2010; Savin et al., 2011; Taniguchi et al., 2011; Wan et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton plays a prominent role in determining chirality in many species.
source: In many species the primary determinant of chirality has been linked to the cytoskeleton with both the microtubule (Nonaka et al., 1998; Ishida et al., 2007) and the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Danilchik et al., 2006; Hozumi et al., 2006; Spéder et al., 2006) (AD Bershadsky, personal communication, November 2013) playing prominent roles.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The actomyosin cytoskeleton plays a prominent role in determining chirality in many species.
source: In many species the primary determinant of chirality has been linked to the cytoskeleton with both the microtubule (Nonaka et al., 1998; Ishida et al., 2007) and the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Danilchik et al., 2006; Hozumi et al., 2006; Spéder et al., 2006) (AD Bershadsky, personal communication, November 2013) playing prominent roles.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies and personal communication.

claim: Myosin motors can rotate actin filaments in motility assays.
source: For example, it has been observed that myosin motors can rotate actin filaments in motility assays (Sase et al., 1997; Beausang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: The posterior and anterior halves of the cortex counter-rotate relative to each other during cortical flow in C. elegans zygotes.
source: Notably, the posterior and anterior halves of the cortex counter-rotate relative to each other (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1), with y-velocities of ∼–2.5 μm/min and ∼1 μm/min respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: Directly observed and measured in experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mean chiral counter-rotation velocity in non-RNAi embryos is −2.9 ± 0.3 μm/min.
source: We find that the distribution of vc is shifted towards negative values, with a mean of −2.9 ± 0.3 μm/min (mean ± error of mean at 99% confidence unless stated otherwise, Figure 1C).
evidence: Quantified from experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Counter-rotating cortical flow breaks chiral symmetry at the 1-cell stage.
source: Thus, counter-rotating cortical flow breaks chiral symmetry at the 1-cell stage, with the posterior half undergoing a counterclockwise rotation when viewed from the posterior pole (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the measured non-zero mean chiral counter-rotation velocity.

claim: The posterior half undergoes a counterclockwise rotation when viewed from the posterior pole.
source: Thus, counter-rotating cortical flow breaks chiral symmetry at the 1-cell stage, with the posterior half undergoing a counterclockwise rotation when viewed from the posterior pole (Figure 1A).
evidence: Determined from the sign of the measured y-velocities.

claim: Chiral counter-rotating flow precedes the previously reported chiral whole-cell rotation of the zygote during cell division.
source: Notably, chiral counter-rotating flow precedes the previously reported chiral whole-cell rotation of the zygote during cell division (Schonegg et al., 2014).
evidence: Temporal relationship inferred from observations and comparison to cited work.

claim: 8 hours of mlc-4 (RNAi) significantly reduces the chiral counter-rotation velocity compared to non-RNAi embryos.
source: We found that 8 hrs of mlc-4 (RNAi) not only reduces the AP flow velocity (Munro et al., 2004) but also significantly reduces vc (Wilcoxon rank sum test at 99% confidence; mean: −1.1 ± 0.4 μm/min, Figure 1C, Video 2) when compared to non-RNAi embryos.
evidence: Measured experimentally and tested for statistical significance.

claim: Chiral flow depends on myosin activity.
source: We conclude that chiral flow depends on myosin activity.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in chiral flow upon mlc-4 RNAi.

claim: Gradients in active tension T along the AP axis drive AP flow.
source: From the structure of Equation 1, we see that gradients in active tension T along the AP axis drive AP flow, while gradients in active torque density τ along the AP axis drive chiral flow orthogonal to the AP axis (Figure 2B, bottom sketch).
evidence: Derived from the theoretical equations of motion for the cortex.

claim: Gradients in active torque density τ along the AP axis drive chiral flow orthogonal to the AP axis.
source: From the structure of Equation 1, we see that gradients in active tension T along the AP axis drive AP flow, while gradients in active torque density τ along the AP axis drive chiral flow orthogonal to the AP axis (Figure 2B, bottom sketch).
evidence: Derived from the theoretical equations of motion for the cortex.

claim: The hydrodynamic length is ℓ=16±0.6 μm.
source: Accordingly, we calculated the theoretical AP and chiral flow profiles from the experimentally determined myosin distribution and found a best match with the experimental profiles for a hydrodynamic length of ℓ=η/γ=16±0.6 μm (Mayer et al., 2010) and an overall chirality index of c = 0.58 ± 0.09 (Figure 2B; see appendix).
evidence: Determined by fitting theoretical model to experimental data.

claim: The overall chirality index is c = 0.58 ± 0.09 for non-RNAi embryos.
source: Accordingly, we calculated the theoretical AP and chiral flow profiles from the experimentally determined myosin distribution and found a best match with the experimental profiles for a hydrodynamic length of ℓ=η/γ=16±0.6 μm (Mayer et al., 2010) and an overall chirality index of c = 0.58 ± 0.09 (Figure 2B; see appendix).
evidence: Determined by fitting theoretical model to experimental data.

claim: A significant part of myosin activity is utilized for generating active torques.
source: We conclude that a significant part of myosin activity is utilized for generating active torques.
evidence: Inferred from the non-zero chirality index c = 0.58.

claim: The handedness of active torques is clockwise when viewed from the outside of the embryo.
source: The handedness of active torques is clockwise when viewed from the outside of the embryo as indicated by the positive sign of the chirality index c.
evidence: Inferred from the positive sign of the chirality index.

claim: The chirality index c remains unchanged at 4 and 6 hours of mlc-4 (RNAi) compared to non-RNAi conditions.
source: While AP flow velocity vx and the chiral flow velocity vc were generally reduced at 4 and 6 hrs of mlc-4 (RNAi) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1–3, Video 3), c remained unchanged from non-RNAi conditions (c, 0.61 ± 0.07 at 4 hrs and 0.52 ± 0.06 at 6 hrs of RNAi, compared to 0.58 ± 0.09 for non-RNAi; Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Measured experimentally and compared statistically.

claim: 8 hours of mlc-4 (RNAi) leads to a significant reduction of the chirality index c.
source: However, 8 hrs of mlc-4 (RNAi) not only resulted in a large reduction of both AP and chiral flow velocities but also led to a significant reduction of c (0.14 ± 0.04, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Measured experimentally and compared statistically.

claim: The overall ratio of active torque density to active tension is not changed by weak reduction of mlc-4 activity.
source: This indicates that the overall ratio of active torque density to active tension is not changed by weak reduction of mlc-4 activity but is altered at stronger RNAi conditions when cortical structure is affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and Video 2).
evidence: Inferred from the unchanged chirality index at 4 and 6 hours of mlc-4 RNAi.

claim: Weak perturbation RNAi of ect-2 leads to a substantial decrease in chiral but not AP flow.
source: We found that weak perturbation RNAi of ect-2 led to a substantial decrease in chiral but not AP flow and thus a decrease in the overall chirality index c when compared to non-RNAi conditions (Figure 3A,D; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 4B, Video 4).
evidence: Measured experimentally and shown in figures.

claim: Weak perturbation RNAi of rga-3 leads to a substantial increase in chiral but not AP flow.
source: Conversely, weak perturbation RNAi of rga-3 led to a substantial increase in chiral but not AP flow and thus an increase in the overall chirality index c (Figure 3A,D; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, Video 5).
evidence: Measured experimentally and shown in figures.

claim: Mild modifications of Rho pathway activity change active torque generation without affecting active tension.
source: We conclude that a principle phenotypical alteration upon mild modifications of Rho pathway activity is a change of the chirality index, or, in other words, mild modifications of Rho pathway activity change active torque generation without affecting active tension.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of ect-2 and rga-3 RNAi on chiral vs AP flow.

claim: In C. elegans, embryonic handedness is determined at the 4-cell stage when the ABa and ABp cells skew clockwise by ∼20°.
source: In C. elegans, embryonic handedness is determined at the 4-cell stage when the ABa and ABp cells skew clockwise by ∼20° (as viewed dorsally in the AP–LR plane, Figure 4A) (Wood, 1991; Bergmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Established fact from cited literature and confirmed in this study.

claim: Chiral cortical flow occurs in ABa at the 4-cell stage with counter-rotation velocity vc = −5.2 ± 1.1 μm/min.
source: Strikingly, we observed chiral cortical flow in ABa, with the cortex in both future daughter cells counter-rotating (vc = −5.2 ± 1.1 μm/min, mean ± error of mean at 95% confidence, Video 6).
evidence: Measured experimentally from video microscopy.

claim: The handedness of chiral flow at the 4-cell stage is identical to that at the 1-cell stage.
source: The handedness of chiral flow is identical to that at the 1-cell stage, indicative of a presence of active torques with the same sign of c.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of flow directions at different stages.

claim: 4.5 hours of ect-2 (RNAi) leads to a significant decrease in chiral flow velocity at the 4-cell stage.
source: We found that 4.5 hrs of ect-2 (RNAi) led to a significant decrease in chiral flow velocity, vc (−3.4 ± 1.4 μm/min), while 4.5 hrs of rga-3 (RNAi) led to a significant increase in vc in the ABa cell (−6.7 ± 0.7 μm/min, Figure 4B, Video 6), similar to our observations at the 1-cell stage.
evidence: Measured experimentally at the 4-cell stage.

claim: 4.5 hours of rga-3 (RNAi) leads to a significant increase in chiral flow velocity at the 4-cell stage.
source: We found that 4.5 hrs of ect-2 (RNAi) led to a significant decrease in chiral flow velocity, vc (−3.4 ± 1.4 μm/min), while 4.5 hrs of rga-3 (RNAi) led to a significant increase in vc in the ABa cell (−6.7 ± 0.7 μm/min, Figure 4B, Video 6), similar to our observations at the 1-cell stage.
evidence: Measured experimentally at the 4-cell stage.

claim: 4.5 hours of ect-2 (RNAi) leads to a significant decrease in skew angle in the ABa cell.
source: Indeed, we found that 4.5 hrs of ect-2 (RNAi) led to a significant decrease in skew (15.8° ± 4.9°) in the ABa cell measured in the AP–LR plane, while 4.5 hrs of rga-3 (RNAi) led to a significant increase in skew (37.8° ± 6.1°) when compared to non-RNAi conditions (23.6° ± 3.7°; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured experimentally and tested for statistical significance.

claim: 4.5 hours of rga-3 (RNAi) leads to a significant increase in skew angle in the ABa cell.
source: Indeed, we found that 4.5 hrs of ect-2 (RNAi) led to a significant decrease in skew (15.8° ± 4.9°) in the ABa cell measured in the AP–LR plane, while 4.5 hrs of rga-3 (RNAi) led to a significant increase in skew (37.8° ± 6.1°) when compared to non-RNAi conditions (23.6° ± 3.7°; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured experimentally and tested for statistical significance.

claim: Changing counter-rotating chiral flow velocity leads to a change in the degree of skew at the 4-cell stage.
source: Thus, changing counter-rotating chiral flow velocity in these cells by weak perturbation of the Rho pathway leads to a change in the degree of skew.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between chiral flow changes and skew angle changes.

claim: Active torque generation and chiral counter-rotating flow participate in the execution of the LR symmetry breaking chiral skew event at the 4-cell stage.
source: This suggests that active torque generation and chiral counter-rotating flow participate in the execution of the LR symmetry breaking chiral skew event at the 4-cell stage.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between chiral flow and skew angle.

claim: RNAi of Wnt signaling genes dsh-2, gsk-3, mig-5, and mom-2 leads to reduced chiral flow and a significant reduction of the overall chirality index c at the 1-cell stage.
source: Strikingly, we found that all these conditions (except mom-5) led to reduced chiral flow and a significant reduction of the overall chirality index c at the 1-cell stage (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2–4, Video 7).
evidence: Measured experimentally for multiple Wnt pathway genes.

claim: There is a fundamental link between genes that affect LR symmetry breaking and chiral counter-rotating flow.
source: These results are indicative of a fundamental link between genes that affect LR symmetry breaking and chiral counter-rotating flow.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of Wnt signaling gene knockdowns on chiral flow.

claim: Active torque generation and chiral counter-rotating flows participate in the establishment of the L/R body axis of C. elegans.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that active torque generation and chiral counter-rotating flows participate in the establishment of the L/R body axis of C. elegans.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of experiments at 1-cell and 4-cell stages.

claim: The actomyosin cytoskeleton in C. elegans generates active chiral torques with clockwise handedness when viewed from the outside of the cell.
source: To conclude, the actomyosin cytoskeleton in C. elegans generates active chiral torques with clockwise handedness when viewed from the outside of the cell.
evidence: Concluded from the positive chirality index and flow patterns.

claim: Active chiral torques drive a specific pattern of chiral flows which can be understood quantitatively based on the physics of active gels with chiral asymmetries.
source: They drive a specific pattern of chiral flows which can be understood quantitatively based on the physics of active gels with chiral asymmetries (Kruse et al., 2005; Fürthauer et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by the agreement between theoretical model and experimental data.

claim: Weak perturbation RNAi experiments indicate that Rho activity affects cortical chirality in a way that does not depend on its role in activating myosin.
source: Furthermore, our weak perturbation RNAi experiments indicate that Rho activity affects cortical chirality in a way that does not depend on its role in activating myosin.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on chiral vs AP flow in Rho pathway perturbations.

claim: Active torques are generated at multiple stages during development, in the zygote during polarity establishment and at the 4-cell stage.
source: Our results imply that active torques are generated at multiple stages during development, in the zygote during polarity establishment, without immediate consequences with respect to LR symmetry breaking, and again at the 4-cell stage, but here as an instructional and mechanistic event that helps to break left/right symmetry.
evidence: Inferred from observations at both 1-cell and 4-cell stages.

claim: The cell cortex is a thin actin gel containing myosin motors and actin binding proteins.
source: The cell cortex, sandwiched between the membrane and cytoplasm, is a thin actin gel containing myosin motors and actin binding proteins (Pollard and Cooper, 1986; Clark et al., 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The embryo does not appear to break azimuthal symmetry with respect to myosin distribution.
source: Thus, we conclude that the embryo does not appear to break azimuthal symmetry with respect to myosin distribution and that chiral flow does not originate from myosin activity gradients along the azimuthal direction.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of myosin intensity differences between top and bottom halves of the embryo.

claim: Chiral flow does not originate from myosin activity gradients along the azimuthal direction.
source: Thus, we conclude that the embryo does not appear to break azimuthal symmetry with respect to myosin distribution and that chiral flow does not originate from myosin activity gradients along the azimuthal direction.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis showing no detectable gradient in myosin fluorescence intensity along the azimuthal direction.

claim: The chiral skew at the 4-cell stage involves rotation in both the AP–LR plane and the DV–LR plane.
source: This illustrates that the chiral skew at the 4-cell stage is more complex than previously reported, with a chiral rotation in the DV–LR plane in addition to the AP–LR plane.
evidence: Demonstrated by measuring skew angles in different planes.

claim: There is an ∼20° skew in the DV–LR plane even for the non-RNAi condition at the 4-cell stage.
source: Interestingly, we detected an ∼20° skew in this plane even for the non-RNAi condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Measured experimentally in the DV-LR plane.

claim: Cortical flow proceeds primarily along the anteroposterior (AP) axis.
source: Flow proceeds primarily along the anteroposterior (AP) axis (x-direction), however, we also observed flow vectors to have a small component in the direction orthogonal to the AP axis (y-direction).
evidence: Observed from particle image velocimetry analysis.

claim: Flow vectors have a small component in the direction orthogonal to the AP axis.
source: Flow proceeds primarily along the anteroposterior (AP) axis (x-direction), however, we also observed flow vectors to have a small component in the direction orthogonal to the AP axis (y-direction).
evidence: Observed from particle image velocimetry analysis.

claim: The y-velocities in the posterior and anterior halves are ∼–2.5 μm/min and ∼1 μm/min respectively.
source: Notably, the posterior and anterior halves of the cortex counter-rotate relative to each other (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1), with y-velocities of ∼–2.5 μm/min and ∼1 μm/min respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: Measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 8 hours of mlc-4 (RNAi) reduces the AP flow velocity.
source: We found that 8 hrs of mlc-4 (RNAi) not only reduces the AP flow velocity (Munro et al., 2004) but also significantly reduces vc (Wilcoxon rank sum test at 99% confidence; mean: −1.1 ± 0.4 μm/min, Figure 1C, Video 2) when compared to non-RNAi embryos.
evidence: Measured experimentally and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Both active tension T and active torque density τ are proportional to the local myosin concentration.
source: We assume that both active tension T and active torque density τ are proportional to the local myosin concentration, leading to a single value of the chirality index c that is constant over the embryo.
evidence: This is an assumption made for the theoretical model.

claim: Weak perturbation of mlc-4 affects both chiral and AP flow.
source: Thus, a weak perturbation of ect-2 and rga-3 affects chiral but not AP flow, unlike a weak perturbation of mlc-4 which affects both.
evidence: Observed from experimental comparisons of different RNAi conditions.

claim: Weak perturbation of ect-2 and rga-3 affects chiral but not AP flow.
source: Thus, a weak perturbation of ect-2 and rga-3 affects chiral but not AP flow, unlike a weak perturbation of mlc-4 which affects both.
evidence: Observed from experimental comparisons of different RNAi conditions.

claim: Similar results for skew angle changes were obtained in ABp as in ABa.
source: Similar results were obtained in ABp (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured experimentally in both cells.

claim: Wnt-induced signals in many systems propagate through Rho GTPases to promote morphological changes.
source: Since Wnt-induced signals in many systems propagate through Rho GTPases to promote morphological changes (Schlessinger et al., 2009), we speculate that these effects are propagated through Rho signaling (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on cited literature and speculation about mechanism.

claim: The effects of Wnt signaling genes on chiral flow are propagated through Rho signaling.
source: Since Wnt-induced signals in many systems propagate through Rho GTPases to promote morphological changes (Schlessinger et al., 2009), we speculate that these effects are propagated through Rho signaling (Figure 3).
evidence: This is speculation based on known Wnt-Rho connections and the observed effects.

claim: Chiral morphogenetic rearrangements have been observed at other stages in C. elegans development.
source: Chiral morphogenetic rearrangements have been observed at other stages in C. elegans development (Pohl and Bao, 2010) and during the first cleavage (Schonegg et al., 2014; Singh and Pohl, 2014), as well as in other systems (Shibazaki et al., 2004; Danilchik et al., 2006; Géminard et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All chiral morphogenetic events might be driven by active torque generation in the actomyosin layer.
source: It is interesting to speculate that all these events might be driven by active torque generation in the actomyosin layer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of this study.

claim: Cortical structure is disrupted by 8 hours of mlc-4 (RNAi).
source: This indicates that the overall ratio of active torque density to active tension is not changed by weak reduction of mlc-4 activity but is altered at stronger RNAi conditions when cortical structure is affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and Video 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A with foci size analysis.

claim: The cell cortex can be described as a thin film of an active chiral fluid.
source: We derive equations of motion for the cell cortex, describing it as a thin film of active chiral fluid (Fürthauer et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is the theoretical framework used in the study, based on cited work.

claim: Molecular force generation by actin and myosin is represented by active force and torque dipoles.
source: In summary, molecular force generation by actin and myosin is represented by active force and torque dipoles.
evidence: This is part of the theoretical framework developed in the appendix.

claim: Active force and torque dipoles give rise to an active tension and an active torque density in the material and can generate flows.
source: These give rise to an active tension and an active torque density in the material and can generate flows.
evidence: This is part of the theoretical framework developed in the appendix.

claim: Spatial gradients in active tension are generated by a spatially inhomogeneous distribution of myosin motors.
source: Spatial gradients in active tension are generated by a spatially inhomogeneous distribution of myosin motors.
evidence: This is part of the theoretical framework and consistent with previous work.

claim: Spatial gradients in active torque density give rise to a flow orthogonal to the gradient of myosin density.
source: Spatial gradients in active torque density on the other hand give rise to a flow orthogonal to the gradient of myosin density (Fürthauer et al., 2013) (see Equation 18) in a direction that is set by the chirality of the torque dipoles in the cell cortex.
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical equations of motion.
